text: The popular answer is to change shape. Add another midfielder. Pull the wingers narrower. Give the full-backs more protection. Those changes may help, but every solution charges a price. More control can isolate the striker. More attacking freedom can expose the double pivot. Push both full-backs and a turnover opens the channels behind them. Keep one at home and the low block becomes harder to stretch. Carrick's best United has lived between order and speed. The current version too often chooses neither: cautious circulation without rest-defence, then desperate attacks without compact pressure behind the ball. The task is not finding one perfect formation. It is teaching the same principles to survive every formation. The answer is not to ban risk. Great teams create risk by pushing numbers forward; they just decide in advance which spaces must remain protected. United's best passages have a clear first defender after the turnover, a midfielder screening the central lane, and a winger close enough to counter-press. Their worst passages have none of those relationships. The diagram changes, but the principle should not. Shape is the surface. Spacing and timing are the actual system.
